items.prompt: In the cake story, what is the software equivalent of the recipe card?
choices: The source code
The operating system install
The timezone setting it uses
The CI server hardware
items.explanation: The card is what you copy around unchanged, which is the code. The kitchens are the environments.

items.prompt: What does environment drift mean?
choices: A server that slowly runs out of memory
Code that changes by itself over time
A network that gets slower each year
Machines that should match have slowly become different
items.explanation: Drift is about the surroundings of the code diverging, not the code changing.

items.prompt: True or false: drift only happens when someone deliberately changes a setting.
choices: True, someone must edit a setting on purpose to cause it
False, separate installs and patches wander apart on their own
True, but only when a developer changes the code first and ships it
items.explanation: Machines installed at different times by different processes drift without anyone deciding to.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT a place where drift hides?
choices: Installed tool versions
The timezone on the machine
The wording of a code comment
A leftover process on a machine
items.explanation: Comments do not change how the program behaves. The other three are properties of the machine.

items.prompt: Why can a code review not catch drift?
choices: A diff shows the code, not the machine it relies on
Drift only shows up after the review has already ended
Reviewers never read the code closely
items.explanation: Review sees what changed in the source. Hidden assumptions about the machine are not in the diff.

items.prompt: Tests pass on a laptop and on CI, but production gives wrong output. Best first question?
choices: Which developer wrote the function?
Why did the tests not crash?
What differs between production and the other two?
Is the code longer than usual?
items.explanation: Same code and different results points at the environment, so compare the environments.

items.prompt: Environment parity means dev, CI and production run:
choices: Roughly similar versions that mostly match
The same hardware size and brand
The same environment, down to runtime and dependency versions
The same team's setup notes
items.explanation: Parity is an exact match of what the code depends on, not an approximate one.

items.prompt: 'Works on my machine' is best read as:
choices: A sign the code depends on something it never declared
Proof that the bug must be in the other machine, not here
Evidence the test suite is too strict
A reason to stop testing locally and only test on CI
items.explanation: It points to an undeclared dependency on that one machine's setup.

items.prompt: Three environments run the same commit. The laptop (Node 20.11) and CI (Node 18.9) pass every test. Production (Node 20.4) returns wrong dates with no error. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The code relies on something the environments do not share, and nothing declares it
The Node versions alone must be the cause, because they differ in all three
Two passing runs prove the code is correct, so production's runtime is faulty
Silent wrong output means the tests needed larger inputs, not a different environment
items.explanation: Identical code with different outcomes points at the surroundings. The versions are suspects but not proven: CI differs the most and passes. The ambient setting (here, timezone) is the real undeclared input.
items.reference:
Same recipe, different kitchen
recipe card = the source code
kitchen = laptop, CI, production
hot oven nobody wrote down = hidden dependency
raw cake = works here, breaks there
Why: the code can be identical while the machine under it is not, and a code diff never shows that.
items.learnMore:
Environment drift

Drift is a difference between machines that should match, grown through separate installs and patches over time. Nobody chooses it and no diff shows it.

Common mistake

Hunting for the bug in the code first. When the code is identical in every place, look at what differs around it.
items.reflection: Think of a process at work or home that only runs well for one person. What do they do that the written steps never mention?

items.prompt: Which statement best separates drift from deliberate configuration?
choices: Drift is always a larger difference than a configuration setting
Drift is a difference nobody chose and nobody can see; configuration is declared
Configuration changes behavior while drift never does
Drift happens at build time and configuration at review time
items.explanation: Both can change behavior. What matters is visibility and intent: a declared setting can be reviewed, drift cannot.

items.prompt: A team keeps a wiki page with the exact versions every environment should have. Why does this fall short of parity?
choices: Written versions need identical hardware vendors to have any effect
Pages cover the runtime only and never the libraries or the settings
Pages go stale, and each machine can diverge from it unnoticed
Pages are reviewed less often than code, so they contain more typos
items.explanation: A page describes the target. Every machine is still set up and patched on its own, and nothing flags a mismatch. Only a single built artifact removes the independent installs.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT an example of drift?
choices: A command-line tool that someone installed by hand on a single CI runner months ago and never recorded
CI images rebuilt every week while developer laptops update every month
Production's database address differs, passed in at launch and recorded in config
A forgotten background process still holding a port on one machine
items.explanation: The address is declared where the container starts, so it is configuration. The other three are unrecorded differences that nobody chose.

items.prompt: A container image bundles:
choices: Only the app's source code
A separate computer's hardware
The app with its runtime and libraries
The developer's editor settings
items.explanation: The point of the image is to carry the app and everything it depends on.

items.prompt: A container is lighter than a VM because it:
choices: Skips the app's libraries entirely when it starts
Runs with no isolation at all from other processes
Shares the host's kernel instead of bringing an OS
Compresses the source files before running them
items.explanation: No guest operating system has to be carried or booted.

items.prompt: Which usually starts faster?
choices: A virtual machine
A container
They are identical
items.explanation: A container starts a process. A VM boots a whole guest OS.

items.prompt: Running the same image on a laptop, CI and production gives:
choices: A different runtime on each host
The same packaged environment each time
Whatever libraries the host has installed
items.explanation: Nothing is taken from the host except the kernel, so the environment is the image's.

items.prompt: Can a VM also deliver parity?
choices: No, VMs cannot package anything
Yes, it also packages one environment
Only if its host runs the same operating system
items.explanation: Both approaches package the environment. They differ in weight and isolation.

items.prompt: What is the difference between an image and a container?
choices: The image is a running copy; the container is the sealed package
The image is the sealed package; the container is a running copy
They are two names for the host operating system
items.explanation: Build the image once, then start as many containers from it as you like.

items.prompt: What do a container and its host share?
choices: The libraries
The app code
The kernel
The dependency tree
items.explanation: Libraries and dependencies come from the image. Only the kernel is the host's.

items.prompt: Why package the environment together with the app?
choices: So the app uses less memory at run time
So no machine can differ in what the app depends on
So the code compiles faster on each machine than before
So tests no longer need to run
items.explanation: The app can only meet what the image holds, so nothing can drift.

items.prompt: A teammate says containers guarantee parity less well than VMs, because containers share the host's kernel. Best reply?
choices: Correct, because a shared kernel means each host supplies different libraries
Correct, because parity needs a separate OS for every instance
Wrong, because containers share nothing with the host, not even the kernel
Parity comes from packaging libraries once; a shared kernel affects isolation
items.explanation: The libraries, runtime and dependencies are in the image regardless. The kernel is a separate matter that touches isolation, not what the app finds installed.
items.reference:
Container versus virtual machine
both: package one environment, same each run
VM: carries a whole guest operating system
container: shares the host's kernel
container: lighter, starts in seconds
Why: parity comes from packaging the environment once, and both do that; the container just carries less.
items.learnMore:
Images and containers

An image is the sealed package: app, runtime, libraries. A container is one running copy of it. Because it shares the host's kernel, a container is light, but the packaged environment is just as fixed as a VM's.

Common mistake

Thinking a shared kernel weakens the parity guarantee. It affects isolation strength, not what the app finds installed.
items.reflection: Where else do you ship something together with everything it needs, so the receiver does not have to set anything up?

items.prompt: The image has Node 20.11 baked in, and the host machine has Node 16 installed. Which Node does the app use?
choices: Node 16, because the host's tools take priority
The newer of the two, chosen at start-up
Both, with their results merged
The baked-in one; the host's installed version is not used
items.explanation: A container resolves the runtime from its own image. Only the kernel comes from the host.

choices: Parity does not decide it, as both package one environment
Containers are required, because only containers give you parity
VMs are ruled out, since they cannot package dependencies
Neither works, because parity needs a shared kernel
items.explanation: Both give the same parity. The isolation depth is a separate trade-off to weigh on its own.

items.prompt: Which is a property of an image, not of a running container?
choices: It is built once and does not change while hosts run it
It holds the data that users created while it was running
It uses CPU and memory on whichever host runs it
It differs slightly between a laptop and production
items.explanation: The image is the sealed, fixed artifact. Running copies are what use resources and accumulate data.

items.prompt: A call to a newer API works locally and fails on CI. Which category?
choices: Runtime version
Leftover port state
Locale setting
Hardware age
items.explanation: CI runs an older runtime that lacks the API.

items.prompt: Dates come out different on one machine only. Likely category?
choices: A runtime version
A busy network port on it
A comment missing from the code
A timezone or locale setting
items.explanation: Date handling reads the machine's clock settings.

items.prompt: 'Connection refused' because a port is already taken. Category?
choices: Runtime version
A locale setting
Leftover state
Hardware age and wear
items.explanation: Something left running on that machine holds the port.

items.prompt: A build step behaves differently depending on who runs it. Category?
choices: Installed tool versions
Leftover state
Locale setting
Operating system brand name
items.explanation: A hand-installed tool is at a different version on each machine.

items.prompt: Why does adding environments raise the risk of drift faster than expected?
choices: Each new one slows the others down
Drift spreads from one machine to the next one
Each one is another chance to have drifted
items.explanation: The chance that at least one differs is one minus the chance that none do.

items.prompt: With an assumed 15% chance per environment, what is the chance one environment has drifted?
items.explanation: With a single environment the chance is just its own.

items.prompt: Why does drift appear without anyone choosing it?
choices: Setups are made at different times and patched separately
Developers secretly edit each other's machines
Code rewrites its own settings
items.explanation: Independent histories diverge by default.

items.prompt: Which is NOT a typical drift source?
choices: A renamed variable in the source code
Operating system library versions
Locale and language settings
Environment variables set by the shell
items.explanation: A renamed variable is a code change, which review can see.

items.prompt: A report prints dates one day off, only on the CI runner, with identical code and input. Which category fits best?
choices: Runtime version: CI must be running an older Node release
Leftover state: another job on the runner is holding the date
Settings: the runner's timezone differs from the others
Installed tools: a date command on the runner differs in version
items.explanation: Same code and input with a different calendar day points to the clock setting, which is a settings category.
items.reference:
Four drift categories
runtime version: newer API fails on older CI
settings (TZ, locale): dates differ on one machine
installed tools: build behaves per runner
leftover state: port already taken
Why: every category lives on the machine, not in the diff, so none are visible to review.
items.learnMore:
Where drift comes from and how fast it grows

Each environment is set up once and patched on its own schedule. If each has some independent chance of having drifted, the chance that at least one has is one minus the chance that none has, which climbs quickly as environments are added.

Common mistake

Treating the risk as additive. Adding 15 points per environment overshoots; the real curve flattens as it nears 100 percent.
items.reflection: Think of a set of copies of anything that were made separately and never compared. How would you find out which ones had changed?

items.prompt: With an assumed independent 15% chance of drift per environment, which is closest to the chance that at least one of 6 has drifted?
items.explanation: One minus 0.85 to the sixth power is about 0.62. Multiplying 6 by 15 gives 90, which ignores overlap.

items.prompt: A fourth environment (staging) is added to three. Under the same assumptions, what happens to the chance that at least one has drifted?

It falls, since more environments allow more cross-checks
It rises from about 39% to about 48%, a smaller step than 15 points
items.explanation: Three gives 38.6 percent and four gives 47.8 percent. The step shrinks as the total approaches 100 percent, but the risk still climbs.

items.prompt: A container image is built:
choices: Fresh on every machine that runs it
Once, then run in many places
Only when a bug appears
items.explanation: One build, many runs, is the whole idea.

items.prompt: Where are dependencies resolved in the image model?
choices: At build time
At run time on each host
At deploy approval time
items.explanation: They are baked in during the single build.

items.prompt: A setup script is run on three machines. How many installs happen?
choices: One in total
Three, one per machine
None, a script only copies files
items.explanation: Each machine runs its own install, at its own time.

items.prompt: Which can differ between environments by design?
choices: The runtime baked into the image
A database address passed in at start
The OS libraries inside the image
The dependency tree inside the image layers
items.explanation: Start-up settings are the intentional variation. The image contents are not.

items.prompt: Settings passed in when a container starts are:
choices: Silent drift
Baked into the image itself, unseen
Declared and reviewable
items.explanation: They are written where the container is launched, so people can see them.

items.prompt: Why is running an image more repeatable than installing?
choices: Running is always faster
Installs are forbidden in tests
Nothing is re-resolved at run time
items.explanation: All resolution already happened at build.

items.prompt: In the kitchen story, a container is closest to:
choices: Shipping the finished counter with its tools
Mailing the recipe card again
Writing a longer recipe
items.explanation: The whole working setup travels, not just instructions.

items.prompt: What does the image deliberately NOT include?
choices: The language runtime
The app code
The dependencies
Per-environment settings such as a database address
items.explanation: Those vary by environment and are passed in at start.

items.prompt: A teammate proposes one thorough setup script run on the laptop, on CI and on production. Why does it fall short of build-once parity?
choices: It still installs three times, once on each machine's state
Scripts cannot pin versions, so each run installs whatever is newest
Scripts can only be executed on the production host
Scripts install the dependencies but skip the runtime
items.explanation: Repeating installation per environment is the pattern that causes drift. A script narrows it but does not remove it.
items.reference:
Install per machine vs build once
setup script: install runs 3 times, on 3 machines
image: dependencies resolved once at build
run: no install step at all
start-up settings: declared, may differ on purpose
Why: drift comes from repeated, independent installs; one build removes the repetition.
items.learnMore:
Resolve once, run everywhere

A container moves dependency resolution from every machine, every time, to one build step. What still varies, like a database address, is passed in when the container starts, where it is visible and reviewable.

Common mistake

Believing a shared setup script gives the same result. It still runs separately on each machine, so the same drift can creep in.
items.reflection: What in your own work gets rebuilt from instructions each time, when it could be built once and handed over finished?

items.prompt: Each environment runs docker build from the same source on its own schedule. Why is that not parity?
choices: Each build resolves dependencies on its own, so images differ
Builds on different machines cannot read the same source tree files
Docker builds ignore the lockfile when they are run outside of CI
Images built outside the production host are rejected by the registry
items.explanation: Building per environment brings back repeated resolution. Build once, then run that same image.

items.prompt: Implement `dayOf(ms, tz)`: return the calendar date (YYYY-MM-DD) of the moment `ms` in the timezone `tz`. Hint: `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-CA", { timeZone: tz })` formats as YYYY-MM-DD. Do not read the host's own timezone.
items.explanation: The timezone arrives as a parameter, so the answer depends only on the inputs and not on the machine.

items.prompt: Implement `hourOf(ms, tz)`: return the hour (0 to 23, as a number) of the moment `ms` in timezone `tz`. Hint: `Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { timeZone: tz, hour: "numeric", hourCycle: "h23" })`.
items.explanation: Formatting in a named zone gives the hour there. The zone is an input, so the result is the same on every machine.

items.prompt: Implement `isSameDay(aMs, bMs, tz)`: true when both moments fall on the same calendar date in timezone `tz`.
items.explanation: Both moments are turned into dates in the same named zone, then compared. The zone is the only thing that decides the answer.

items.prompt: Implement `isWeekend(ms, tz)`: true when the moment falls on a Saturday or Sunday in timezone `tz`. Hint: `Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { timeZone: tz, weekday: "short" })` gives "Sat" or "Sun".
items.explanation: The same instant is a different weekday in different zones, so the zone has to be passed in.

items.prompt: Implement `greetingFor(ms, tz)`: return "morning" for hours 0 to 11, "afternoon" for 12 to 17, and "evening" for 18 to 23 in timezone `tz`.
items.explanation: The hour is read in the named zone, then bucketed. One instant gives different greetings in different zones.

items.prompt: Implement `joinPath(parts, sep)`: join the strings in `parts` with the separator `sep`, which is passed in instead of read from the operating system.
items.explanation: A path separator is another ambient fact that differs per operating system. Passing it in keeps the result the same everywhere.

items.prompt: Implement `isoDay(ms)`: return the UTC calendar date of `ms` as YYYY-MM-DD. Hint: `new Date(ms).toISOString()` is always in UTC.
items.explanation: toISOString always reports UTC, so it does not depend on the machine's timezone.

items.prompt: Implement `minutesSince(thenMs, nowMs)`: the whole number of minutes between the two moments. The current time arrives as `nowMs`; do not read the clock yourself.
items.explanation: Passing the current time in makes the function repeatable. Reading the clock inside would make it depend on when it runs.

items.prompt: Implement `isToday(timestampMs, timezone, nowMs)`: true when the two moments fall on the same calendar date in `timezone`. The function must not read the host's timezone or the current time.
items.explanation: Both the zone and the current time are inputs, so the function gives the same answer on a laptop in New York and a server in UTC.
items.reference:
Make the hidden input an argument
ambient: host timezone, clock, path separator
explicit: pass zone, now, separator in
same inputs, same answer on any machine
TZ=UTC on CI only moves the problem
Why: correctness should not depend on anything outside what you built and tested.
items.learnMore:
Ambient inputs

A function that reads the host's timezone or clock is secretly taking an extra argument. Naming that argument in the signature makes the function repeatable, testable and safe to move between machines.

Common mistake

Fixing it by setting the same timezone on every machine. That is still an ambient setting, easy to forget on the next one.

items.prompt: npm ci differs from npm install in that it:
choices: Installs exactly the lockfile's tree and fails on mismatch
Skips the dependency step entirely during every build
Updates every package to its newest version before installing
items.explanation: That strictness is what makes builds repeatable.

items.prompt: Why copy the package files before the rest of the source?
choices: So source files load first
So the install layer is reused when only source changes
So secrets get encrypted
items.explanation: Layer caching: the install only reruns if the manifests change.

items.prompt: Which is a more precise way to name a base image?
choices: A moving tag
A version number
A digest
items.explanation: A digest is a hash of the exact bytes.

items.prompt: A tag such as node:20.11 can be:
choices: Never changed by anyone once it is published
Edited only by you
Re-pointed to a different image
items.explanation: Tags are labels a registry owner can move.

items.prompt: Does a container image cover the database schema?
choices: No, it is outside the image
Yes, the image carries its own schema
Only when the schema is copied in at build time
items.explanation: The schema lives in the database, not in the image.

items.prompt: Should secrets be baked into the image?
choices: Yes, for stronger parity
No; pass them in when the container starts
Yes, but only in production
items.explanation: Baking them in forces one image per environment.

items.prompt: What does 'parity layer by layer' mean?
choices: If the application layer matches, the layers below it must match as well
Only the top layer of the stack needs to match
Check each layer separately; parity in one does not carry over
If one layer matches, all of them do
items.explanation: A matching image says nothing about a different database or partner API.

items.prompt: Which is outside a container's guarantee?
choices: The OS libraries in the image
The language runtime
Dependencies
A partner API's behavior
items.explanation: The partner runs elsewhere, so the image cannot pin it.

items.prompt: A teammate swaps npm ci for npm install in the image definition. Which guarantee is loosened?
choices: The image can no longer be started on a developer laptop
The base image tag stops being looked up at build time
Dependencies stop being installed during the build, so the image runs empty
Two builds of the same commit can contain different dependency versions
items.explanation: npm install may resolve newer matching versions if the registry changed, so repeated builds can differ.
items.reference:
What an image pins, and what it cannot
npm ci: exact lockfile tree, fails on mismatch
digest: fixed bytes; tag: a movable label
inside image: OS libs, runtime, dependencies
outside: database schema, partner APIs, kernel
Why: repeatable builds need pinned inputs, and parity only covers what is inside the image.
items.learnMore:
Pinning and the edge of the guarantee

An image build still reads from outside: a base image name and a package registry. Pin the install with the lockfile and the base image with a digest. After that, remember the guarantee stops at the image boundary.

Common mistake

Declaring parity solved after containerizing. A database, a partner service or the host network can still differ.
items.reflection: Which of your own systems depends on something outside the part you control, and how would you notice if it changed?

items.prompt: Staging behaves differently from production because a partner's test API returns different data, although both run the same image. What does this show?
choices: The image was built incorrectly and must be rebuilt from a clean checkout
The image only covers what is inside it; the partner service is outside
Staging and production need different base images
Parity only works when staging runs as a VM
items.explanation: The image cannot pin a service running elsewhere, so that layer must be reasoned about separately.
